Two weeks after his uncharacteristically spicy comments on the demise of BioWare, Spector's anger clearly has not subsided.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two weeks after literally calling "bullshit" on EA's decision to close BioWare, immsim legend Warren Spector has posted a follow-up message on LinkedIn that avoids the spicy language but sounds angrier than ever.

"I recently posted my thoughts about EA’s shuttering of BioWare," Spector wrote. "Those of you who read my post know that I was unhappy. I remain so.

"The tragedy of so many layoffs the last few years hasn’t been lost on me, but for some reason, BioWare hit me on an emotional level nothing before had. I was gut-punched."

But some readers, he continued, replied to say that BioWare's best days were behind it, and that shutting it down was a "sound business decision." Those reactions appear to have re-stoked Spector's rage, as he said those people missed his actual complaint: That the game industry executives who are responsible for these problems are never the ones to suffer the consequences.

"If studio-level people leave, resulting in dilution of talent, someone is creating an environment that pushes them out. Do those culture-killers pay any price?" Spector wrote in his new message. "If executives misread the market, over-hire, or make decisions that result in under-funded, over-funded, poorly-marketed games, do they lose sleep, let alone jobs? Do those same executives suffer like developers when the needs of financial partners and investors take precedence over players, does anyone up there care?

"Is there ANY accountability left in this world?"

Then he took direct aim at Electronic Arts' C-suite with some very large, ugly numbers:

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Those figures represent the total compensation given to EA's executives in its 2026 fiscal year—a single 12-month period. They're also significant increases over the previous year: Wilson, for instance, got $30.5 million in 2025, while Miele's was given $9.1 million.

Ironically, those EA executive salaries aren't even directly related to the BioWare closure. Wilson's $8 million raise (and all the others), which was awarded in part for "meeting all milestones for a high-quality launch of Battlefield 6," came just a few months after laying off employees at the studios that made it—Criterion, Dice, Ripple Effect, and Motive—and entirely shuttering Ridgeline Games, which had been working on a new, more story-focused Battlefield game.

"Tens of thousands of do-ers and makers are out of work and these people think they're worth that kind of compensation?" Spector concluded. "And if you think this is a discussion about 'sound business decisions' I hope you never get anywhere near running a business. Or at least that people have the sense not to go work for you."

Spector's frustration and anger comes through here even more clearly than it did when he dropped his uncharacteristic curse, because it's focused: Waving our hands and bemoaning the bullshit might be briefly cathartic, but pointing the finger at these guys over here and saying "this is why" brings the problem into focus like the sun through a magnifying glass.

Sadly, pushback on compensation packages of this size are extremely rare. An analyst report in 2020, when EA shareholders took the unusual step of rejecting a proposed pay hike for the company's executives, said the failure rate of such proposals was just 2.7% in 2019, and 2.6% in 2018. Wilson was paid more than $21 million that year.

#3905. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#3904. Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble canceled

Free-to-play multiplayer arena shooter Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble has been canceled, publisher Sony Interactive Entertainment and developer Oh BiBi announced.

The game soft-launched for iOS and Android in the Philippines and Indonesia alongside its announcement in November 2025, followed by Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark in December 2025, Canada in May 2026, and the United Kingdom in August 2026.

In a message posted to the game’s official website, Oh BiBi said a final update is being released today, and the game will be removed from storefronts on November 21. Servers will officially close on May 1, 2027.

■ Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble Update (November 6, 2026)

We’ve made the difficult decision to cease development of Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble.

The final planned update will be rolling out November 6, 2026, and the app will be removed from stores on November 21, 2026.

Players who already have the game will be able to continue playing until May 1, 2027, when the game’s servers will permanently shut down.

On behalf of the dev team and everyone helping to make the game, thanks to our amazing community for all your support, especially to those who have spent time playing, sharing feedback, and helping shape Ranger Rumble throughout its development!

Game servers will permanently shut down on May 1, 2027.

Can I continue playing after the game is removed from stores?

If you already installed the game, you will be able to continue playing the game until End of Service on May 1, 2027.

Will I still be able to download and reinstall the game?

If you’re an existing player, Yes, until November 21, 2026, after that the game will be delisted from Apple’s App Store and Google Play.

Will the game still work after the servers have been shut down?

No, once the game servers are shutdown on May 1, 2027, the game will no longer load.

Will there be any additional game updates?

No, there are no planned updates after November 7, 2026.

Will existing game modes, multiplayer matchmaking and competitive features remain available?

All current game modes, matchmaking and competitive features will remain active until End of Service on May 1, 2027.

Will there be any final events, rewards or opportunities to unlock content?

The Qwark Pass seasons will continue to run until May 1, 2027, and the Super Pass is now free, and all content can be earned throughout each season.

What happens to my Quark Pass and any unclaimed rewards?

You have until End of Service on May 1, 2027, to enter, claim and utilize any rewards earned through play.

No, in-app purchases have been removed. You can continue to earn rewards through play and spending that currency on upgrades, cosmetics, characters and currencies.

What happens to my unused in-game currency?

You have until End of Service on May 1, 2027, to use any currency you’ve earned or purchased.

Can I request a refund for previous purchases?

Your eligibility for a refund for any purchases made will be through Apple’s App Store or Google Play.

What happens to my account and game progress after shut-down?

All player data will be wiped from the servers at the End of Service, May 1, 2027. If you want to delete your data ahead of May 1, 2027, you can contact support here.

Can I transfer my progress, purchases or unlocked items to another game?

No, your progress and items are not transferable to any other game.

What happens if I registered for the game or earned pre-registration rewards?

Pre-registration rewards will be available to all players logging into the November 7, 2026 update.

What happens to my personal data after the game closes?

All player data will be deleted at End of Service, on May 1, 2027.

Does this affect other Ratchet & Clank games or PlayStation services?

No, Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble‘s ceasing development has no impact on other Ratchet & Clank games or PlayStation services.

#3903. Yakuza creator's new studio and its debut game Gang of Dragon are no more after losing funding from NetEase

Nagoshi Studio has officially shut down and its first game called Gang of Dragon is seemingly no more, months after publisher NetEase pulled funding from the Yakuza-like project.

Toshihiro Nagoshi (often cited as the creator of the brilliant Yakuza and Like A Dragon game series) opened his new studio in 2021 and announced his next game with a very familiar title almost one year ago. Now, the Tokyo-based developer has closed its doors, as confirmed in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

The news comes months after employees were told that the studio's future was at risk due to NetEase's funding cuts. Nagoshi Studio reportedly needed another £33.1 million (about $44.4m at the time) to get Gang of Dragon past the finish line - a paycheck NetEase purportedly didn't want to cough up.

The China-based Marvel Rivals and Where Winds Meet publisher has been significantly scaling back on international investments these past few years. Visions of Mana developer Ouka Studios was shut down just after launching its gorgeous action game, Worlds Untold (a studio formed by Mass Effect veteran Mac Walters) had to pause operations to find a new partner, and Halo Infinite lead Jerry Hook's studio also ran into very similar issues last year.

Some developers have been a little luckier. Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture saved itself with a management buyout and now operates as an independent developer, for one.

Not much is known about Gang of Dragon, but its debut trailer featured the violent crime and high drama you'd expect from Nagoshi's previous work. The game also starred Ma Dong-seok, the acclaimed actor you might recognise from films such as Train to Busan and Marvel's Eternals.

#3902. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#3901. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.

#3900. Days Gone studio's next PlayStation exclusive to be revealed and released in 2027, according to new report

Sony's Bend Studio, perhaps one of its lesser discussed development houses, has apparently been deep in development on its next title. The game is reportedly set to be announced in 2027, and released in the same year.

That's according to MP1st, citing "people aware of what's happening at Bend". Like Days Gone, Bend's next game is in third-person. The title is said to include co-op support, but no live service elements.

The report doesn't say whether the game is based on a new IP or an existing one, but it does state that it's not a sequel to Days Gone. The game is apparently "much further along in development" than we realise, which isn't entirely surprising considering Bend has been quiet for years.

The seven years since the release of Days Gone in 2019 have been tumultuous for Bend Studio. The developer revealed in 2022 its next project is a new IP that "builds upon the open-world systems of Days Gone" and includes multiplayer elements.

Two years later, a job post described a game in development at Bend as a triple-A live service project. That unannounced game was then cancelled in 2025, triggering a wave of layoffs at the studio that took place a few months later. Bend hasn't said a word since then.

It's now clear the studio hopped on its next project following the cancellation of that live service game. Seeing as 2026 is nearly over, we're not likely to be waiting much longer to see that mysterious game unveiled.

#3898. "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"

Unionised workers reiterate call for a "solid offer" for Arkane Lyon's future

Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Published by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - one of two unions who represent workers at Arkane, the other being Printemps écologique, who didn't issue a similar message - the official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine". It maintains that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. The writers then take Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuse the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 11th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.

#3897. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.

Hidemaro Fujibayashi wants to make sure younger staff "don't feel like they need to pull from an already existing pool of ideas that Zelda has plotted"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi says future games in the series shouldn't rely on reheating Breath of the Wild or Ocarina of Time's ideas.

Speaking to Polygon, Fujibayashi – who served as director of Capcom's Oracle games and The Minish Cap, before joining Nintendo where he would go on to develop Skyward Sword, Breath of the Wild, and Tears of the Kingdom – explained why Zelda games are often reinventing the series. "These are all ideas or nuggets of ideas that developers at that time feel like, 'okay, this is going to be fun,'" Fujibayashi says, adding, "I feel like Zelda creates this foundation, this arena where developers can bring those ideas and actually bring them to life and realize that."

Not all Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake devs have played the N64 original – with Eiji Aonuma saying the remake pretty much served as an exercise for the developers who hadn't to see what insight it brings them.

Fujibayashi notes that "A lot of times, the question I have when I talk to younger staff is like, 'Is that going to be fun?'" and that he would point out if these ideas were previously done in the likes of Breath of the Wild or Ocarina of Time, which he notes is "the kind of probing and discussion that we do with the team such that they don't feel like they need to pull from an already existing pool of ideas that Zelda has plotted."

We currently don't know what the future of the Zelda series holds. Many – myself included – expect the open-world formula established in Breath of the Wild, and expanded on by Tears of the Kingdom will continue into something new, but from what Fujibayashi says, Zelda can pretty much be anything it wants, so there's a chance we have no idea what form the series may take next.

#3895. Remedy revenue soars by 226% following release of Control Resonant, the developer's fastest-selling game ever

Remedy - the developer behind the recently released Control Resonant - has released a scorcher of a quarterly financial report. It shows that following Resonant's release in September, the company's revenue surged by 226 percent, bringing in €39.6m in Q3.

This performance was described as "a defining milestone for the company" by CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon. The company reported a €0.6m operating profit this quarter, a fair leap upwards from the €16.4m loss from this time last year.

There are some interesting highlights to this sudden surging performance. For one, the US made up nearly half of Control Resonant's players across PC and console, followed by Chinese-speaking regions and then the UK.

Perhaps most crucially is that nearly half of Control Resonant's players were entirely new to the franchise, with the company stating: "Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy."

Control (2019) also saw a bump up in sales thanks to the release of Control Resonant, showing a stronger performance this quarter than the past two quarters this year as well as its comparison period (this quarter last year).

Remedy's CEO now believes the focus for the studio is to "get Resonant into the hands of more players." He continues to say the game has provided a solid foundation for growth as other projects (including the Max Payne 1 & 2 remake) are in the works. In short, things appear to be looking rather good for Remedy.

Control Resonant was an artistically impressive but critically divisive game. While many praised the series' adventure into third person action, some felt it had less of a narrative bite than its predecessor. Nonetheless the game quickly blasted past one million sales after launch.

#3894. You can now play Pillars of Eternity and Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire with a controller on PC from start to finish, thanks to a new update open for testing

Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also gotten a makeover

After gifting Pillars of Eternity a turn-based mode for its tenth anniversary, Obsidian have now rolled out full PC controller support for both the RPG and its younger sibling Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire. The support, along with some tweaks to Deadfire's turn-based mode, are currently out in public test form.

"You can now play the whole of either game with a controller, from character creation to the end credits (and, in Deadfire, all the way out to naval combat), in both real-time with pause and turn-based mode," the studio wrote in their announcement of the public test going live. "Deadfire’s support builds on the controller scheme from the console editions. Prefer to switch things up? Pick up your mouse and keyboard at any time, and the game follows right along."

"Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also been reworked with the improvements we made for Pillars of Eternity’s turn-based mode: turns now follow each character’s speed, combat is more lethal, and swapping weapons or drinking potions no longer costs your action. You can now switch turn-based mode on or off during a playthrough, and the update brings a long list of fixes across combat, quests, audio, and the interface."

Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are included in the support, along with the Steam Deck and Steam's Big Picture mode. Radial menus have been worked in to allow rapid firing of abilities, spells, and party commands, with the interface also popping up the right button prompts for your controller of choice.

These additions are all part of Patch 1.3.10.0, the full notes for which can be found in the post I've embedded above, alongside instructions on how to get into the public test. The patch also does things like ensure "the description of Fulvano’s Boots is no longer fragmented". I'm glad Obsidian have saved those soles.

The studio haven't put a concrete end date on the test at this point, instead noting it "will run for some time as we continue to update it in preparation for a full release". As it's a test, those jumping in should expect bugs and other funkiness.

An updated version of the Xbox PC app available to Xbox Insiders loads up to 60% faster, and it's got some other nice improvements too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Xbox has joined the 'faster launcher load times' arms race, announcing that its updated Xbox PC app, available now to Xbox Insiders, launches up to 60% faster, and has also been overhauled to offer "simpler navigation, updated filters, and new ways to organize your games."

Along with the faster launch time, Xbox said the home, store, and Game Pass pages in the updated app load up to 50% faster, while in-app windows open up to 65% faster—depending upon factors including device, internet connection, system configuration, and usage, of course. Library navigation has been simplified, search has been improved, and friends and social features are now part of the main navigational window.

Credit where it's due: That change to friends and social features is welcome. I don't use the Xbox App much—to be blunt, it's pretty much exclusively for Sea of Thieves. But after a long stretch away from it, I recently jumped back in for some high seas adventures with the crew, and I'll tell you this: Figuring out how to connect with my fellow online swashbucklers was kind of a headache compared to the super-simplicity of Steam. It worked fine, it just wasn't smooth and easy, so anything that helps with that, I'm happy to take.

I'm less excited about the faster loading times. Not that I'm going to complain about performance improvements, I'm just not sure it matters in the grand scheme of things. When the Epic Games Store promised that its "vibe coded" launcher was faster than Steam, a common reaction was mockery: Much of that was sparked by Epic's insistent banging of the 'AI is inevitable' drum, but there was also a lot of 'who cares?' in the reactions, too. I think the Xbox PC app may face the same: Faster is good, sure, but is it going to convince many PC gamers to use it instead of Steam when they don't have to? Of this, I have doubts.

(Steam also recently dropped a performance update that promises to improve loading times as well, blunting the impact of both the Epic and Xbox boosts even further.)

If you want to check out the updated app for yourself, you'll need to be in the Xbox Insiders program—for that, you'll need to install the Xbox Insider Hub. A "refreshed Xbox web experience" is also on the way, with an improved library tab, more efficient use of screen space, and light, dark, and high-contrast visual modes.

#3891. We're going to be recommending the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited a lot from now on, here's why

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Put simply, the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is the best controller currently occupying a space on the shelves. It takes what was already the most premium-feeling gamepad, ports it to PlayStation, and improves upon it with TMR thumbsticks. Every button press, every time you pick up the controller, and every setting easily managed via its onboard display system oozes class, convenience, and money well spent. In a $200 controller market, it's one of the only ones that feels like it offers the full package. If you can afford it, there's no other controller I'd recommend more.

Same best-in-class button actuation as the Xbox version

No option for symmetrical thumbstick fans

Only a mobile companion app, not a PC one

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

The best PS5 controllers have been a bit behind the times lately. While Xbox has been licensing all sorts of third parties to develop gamepads with built-in screens and fancy charging stands, Sony has only just been allowing a few of its favorite brands to create secondary controllers for the PS5 - and still isn't letting any of them have rumble, haptic feedback, or wake privileges - all so that the DualSense seems more special.

Nacon is the third brand to take a second crack at its PS5 controller after Razer and Scuf. The Nacon Revolution 5 Pro was a really great attempt, providing a robust product that was good, but not quite headline-stealing. Nacon then went to Xbox, improved its design, and launched the Revolution X Unlimited, maybe one of the only controllers to ever make me feel like it's worth every penny of its $200 price tag. Now, Nacon is back to PlayStation with an even more refined version, and it's nothing if not a showstopper.

The improved, TMR-wielding Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited takes all of the excellent design, premium feel, and beautiful versatility of the RXU, and makes a renewed claim for the top of the controller market. This time, it argues its case even better than before. If you can afford a £179.99 / $229 controller, you'd be hard-pressed to find a better one than this.

Sometimes, when you go from a first-party controller to a licensed third-party one, things can feel a little foreign. No matter the price, because its design is a different spin on what you're used to, it can still feel like an unofficial knock-off. The Nacon R5U doesn't exactly feel like the DualSense or DualSense Edge, but it has an ability to make you feel like you're right at home.

The controller rests in my hands and fades into my subconscious, placing all of the buttons where I need them to be, and allowing me to focus on the game I'm playing. It doesn't feel like there's an adjustment to make or quirks to get used to; this is controller design at its best. Again, if you're familiar with the Xbox version, you're essentially getting the exact same gamepad design, just with PlayStation embellishments, but I'll give you a brief rundown of what that means.

The R5U has all the standard buttons you'll need to play games on PS5 or PC, along with six extra ones for you to do with what you choose. Four back buttons are on the grips of the controller, and two additional bumpers are up on the shoulders. All of these, barring the R1 and L1 buttons and their accompanying triggers, are microswitches; clicky buttons that provide a snappier feel and more tactile actuation.

The RXU and R5U do those a bit differently than other controllers though - they have a super light actuation with a shorter travel distance than you might be used to elsewhere.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

The result is a controller that feels tactile and unique, while also providing depth and speed in equal measure - a combination which is almost impossible for other controllers to nail at once. It's easy to use and it all responds to your twitchy presses almost as quickly as you think about pushing them down. Every button and material used doesn't feel like an imitation either; this thing feels more premium than any controller by Sony or Microsoft I've held.

The grips are covered in a rubberized texture that has a softening and cooling effect. There's matte plastic paneling elsewhere, but your brain blurs it all into one, and the combination of the grip shapes, materials, and ergonomics at play adds up to a really expensive-feeling peripheral. In short, it's a bloody comfortable gamepad to hold.

What's a shame about the PlayStation version is that it doesn't make the same changes as Razer's Wolverine V3 Pro did when it ported over to the Razer Raiju V3 Pro. Thumbsticks here are asymmetrical, which is welcome for a load of gamers, but isn't exactly authentic to PlayStation. That's hardly a disaster, but I'd love to see a symmetrical version at some point, even if it isn't necessarily Nacon's go-to style.

Nacon's R5U is the first PS5 controller to sport a built-in screen and menu system. In the Xbox and PC controller realm, this is hardly a new feature, but given PlayStation's licensing requires a touchpad to be present, I imagine it's been hard for any brand to really crack the code on Sony's console.

As it happens, Nacon has a clever workaround for this. The touchpad isn't present, but there are six extra buttons in play, and you can map the touchpad function to any of the others. It's hardly a perfect solution, and I wonder whether making the display touchscreen would have been too much of an expense, as it would really have solved the issue beautifully.

That's not the only licensing parameter Nacon has managed to sidestep, however. You may remember from the brand's previous Nacon Revolution 5 Pro controller for PS5 that vibration motors were, in fact, present, but were locked to working in the PC mode only. The same is true here, which again isn't a perfect solution, but does make it the only other PS5-licensed controller that actually has vibration motors in it. The rest of the pack can end up feeling lighter and less up to that $200 price tag as a result.

Speaking of weight, you can adjust the heft here just like with all other flagship Nacon controllers by putting tiny, provided dumbbells into the grips. Combine that with some swappable thumbstick tops, stick widths, and a charging stand, and you get a controller that feels very feature-rich. Would I say the Victrix Pro BFG does an even better job of providing swappable parts? Yes, absolutely, but I think for most gamers, your needs are going to be covered here.

The most notable upgrade from the Nacon Revolution X Unlimited is that the thumbsticks here are TMR, not Hall effect. That gives it a bit more futureproofing, precision, and speed, and means that, for PC players, I'd default to the PS5 version, seeing as they're likely going to work out at the same price for the next little while. That said, both models have a max polling rate of 1,000Hz on PC, which is more than enough for most gamers. It's a shame the ceiling hasn't been raised slightly for the upgraded model to complement its TMR thumbsticks though. Both the RXU and R5U will be locked to 250Hz on their respective consoles anyway, sadly.

Interestingly, Nacon hasn't made a PC companion app this time around; it's opted to make a mobile-only version. I'm not sure what's caused this - perhaps there have been cost limitations, staff changes due to Nacon's current financial troubles, or Nacon really is basing it on feedback from customers.

I can see the usefulness of a mobile app for PS5 players, especially seeing as not all of them will have a PC they can easily connect to. Still, for a controller with a built-in menu system, I feel like any need for additional companion software would probably be for more in-depth things that PC players would like to deep-dive into. Would it really be impossible to make an app for mobile and PC? Or to make the R5U compatible with Nacon's existing PC software for the Xbox model?

I've compared the onboard controls 1:1 to the Xbox version of the controller, and they're exactly the same. A quick tap of the menu button will bring you to options on audio, joysticks, mapping, and settings. Audio is where you can control the R5U's nifty Bluetooth, because these controllers are capable of being paired as separate devices in their own right to channel audio directly through the gamepad. That allows you to adjust mic gain right from the controller's menu.

In "Joysticks", you'll get a sub-menu for the left and right thumbsticks where you can choose input curves, set deadzone levels, and access special settings like the shooter mode and sensitivity plus option. You can even invert the sticks if that's your thing. The last section in this menu is for the gyro controls. Again, these aren't my thing, but that need is covered if it's your preferred way to play.

Button mapping is a fairly obvious one; you can set all of the extra buttons up via shortcuts, but options for mapping PC controls aren't there, so maybe check out the Steam Controller if that sort of thing means a lot to you. I set the touchpad shortcut up to be mapped to the share button, so if you can do without that functionality on PS5, I'd recommend it so you don't lose out on an extra button for in-game stuff.

In "Settings", you can see Bluetooth, pairing, vibration, and battery savings menus.

So, from my assessment, what you can't do on the controller itself and will need the app for is changing the RGB lighting ring on the right stick, diving deeper into profiles, stick response curves, and the rather confusing advanced and custom modes. All in all, it's a pretty handy menu onboard, and one that'll probably prevent most users from needing the mobile app.

To get this out of the way quickly, I've only had one bizarre tech problem with the R5U, and it may be a result of mine being an early sample for reviews. I paired it with its wireless USB dongle out of the box, but I'm not sure the two communicate all that well with one another. If I leave the dongle plugged into the same PC I was connected to last time, boot up the computer, and then the controller, it won't pair with the dongle. I'll need to take out and re-insert the dongle for it to pair with the R5U. That's a bit of an annoyance, and not ideal. It's not an issue I've had with the two different RXU models I've tested though, so I wonder if this might be a quirk of firmware or the early model I received for testing. Other than that, I've had absolutely no problems with the controller.

If I'm brutally honest, besides the charging stand and built-in display, the Nacon R5U isn't offering loads of stuff that other PS5 Pro controllers on the shelves are, so people might struggle to see why the R5U is the undisputed king of the market in my eyes.

I don't think Nacon is offering masses of things you can't get elsewhere, but I do think its version of those things is better than what else is out there. Naturally, a lot of this stuff is going to come down to subjective preferences, right? I review a new controller every week or so and have done so for about four years now, but I accept that I have my own likes and dislikes and yours will be different. All I can tell you is why the R5U has been outshining all the others for me.

Personally, it's because I compare it to other controllers I previously considered the best in certain categories, and it takes the fight to pretty much all of them. There are versatile, jack-of-all-trades peripherals out there, but few do everything this well.

For example, the Razer Wolverine V3 Pro has probably the best microswitch responsiveness of any controller I've come across. If someone was asking me for a controller recommendation based solely on clicky buttons, the V3 Pro, and by proxy, the Raiju V3 Pro, are the ones that spring to mind immediately. They just feel incredibly speedy when playing a fighting game like Dragon Ball Sparking Zero. The RXU and R5U manage to match that responsiveness with equally clicky buttons, and I'd argue they go a step beyond because their actuation is so much friendlier on your thumbs. The buttons here are more cushioned; they have a lighter pressing force requirement, and they opt for a wider, flatter shape. The Asus ROG Raikiri II has a very similar feel to the Wolverine V3 Pro, but its buttons, having more of a domed shape, result in them feeling like they dig into your thumbs more when you press them.

If someone asked me what controller was best for game feel and haptic feedback, I'd be remiss if I didn't recommend the DualSense Edge. The R5U sadly doesn't have access to Sony's homegrown tech in a game like Marvel's Spider-Man 2 on PC, and it for sure lacks the subtlety and detail of proper haptic feedback. Sadly, the R5U's vibration is either on or off, but at the same time, I'd argue there's more to game feel than just feedback through rumble and haptics. Part of game feel is how it mechanically feels to push a button and experience the result of your in-game action on screen (there's a great book called Game Feel by Steve Swink I'd recommend reading if you're a sicko and you're interested in this sort of thing). The R5U's buttons feel better to press than the DualSense's, so while the detail of feedback might not be so strong, you get added extras in the comfort area that I'd argue add up to an interesting match.

If someone asked me for a controller to use purely for driving games, I'd probably point them toward the Thrustmaster eSwap series. That brand treats racing games like a religion, and even if there are other controllers that feel good for driving, it's hard not to think of Thrustmaster as the go-to. The triggers on the R5U are bold, wide, and feel great to accelerate and brake with through the Japanese roads of Forza Horizon 6. I'd hardly say the R5U is a sim racing alternative, but I imagine it would feel great to use driving around the streets of GTA 6.

For competitive FPS games, I'd go to war any day with the FlyDigi Apex 5 thanks to its excellent thumbstick tension and really well-designed back buttons. Now, if I were heading into a virtual gunfight, the R5U would be coming with me. The TMR thumbsticks and extra shooter and sensitivity+ modes on the R5U are unparalleled. I've tested TMR controllers at 8,000Hz polling rates in my favorite shooter, Hunt: Showdown. I've tested the Apex 5; I've tested all sorts of other Hall and TMR controllers in it. I've never experienced mouse-like tracking as I have with the 8K options like the GameSir G7 Pro 8K, and I've not experienced the satisfying flicky tension of the Apex 5. But with the R5U, everything about the controller comes together to form a precision nightmare for any target in my crosshair. I can track well thanks to TMR tech, I can access loads of in-game functions thanks to six extra buttons, and I can make tiny micro adjustments or go for bold flicks and not feel like the controller is the thing letting me down.

I almost always swap for the taller thumbstick option when getting to this part of testing, but in all honesty, I didn't feel I needed it here, and that should tell you everything you need to know about how good this gamepad is in FPS games. And okay, the R5U isn't a match for the modular design of the Victrix Pro BFGs, but letting you adjust weights in the grips, letting you swap thumbstick tops, and offering a carry case with a charging stand and six extra buttons to make use of gives it almost all of the versatility you'll need.

I was actually using the FlyDigi Apex 5, my previous favorite controller for PC gaming, before testing this one. I've been playing my way through Control Resonant, and having six extra buttons is a massive help for its often repetitive combat. But I actually found that the harder actuation force of the Apex 5's buttons was starting to cause fatigue and a bit of strain. Switching to the lighter and easier-to-press buttons of the R5U was so much better. The back buttons are exactly where I need them to be to press easily, but they click with this degree of forgivingness to your hands that makes them actually feel worth the money you've spent. All the while, unlike the SteelSeries Aeon Pro, they don't massively intrude on the design language of the controller - they blend in really nicely.

There's a chance that because these ones are easier to press, you might get more accidental mis-presses, but that hasn't happened to me yet. Remember, you can always map them to be blank if they bother you.

Even battery life has been absolutely stellar. I've tested the R5U for about two or three weeks now, and despite all the use I've gotten out of it, it's only just started signalling that its battery is low.

A week or two ago, I saw people in the Controller sub-Reddit saying that you shouldn't give your hard-earned cash to big companies like Razer, Nacon, SteelSeries, Sony, and Microsoft. "The GameSir G7 Pro gives you everything you need for less than half the price", they argued, "so why give all that money to brands who just don't care about the controllers they make."

The GameSir G7 Pro is a truly excellent controller, and one that I'd recommend to most people based on pure value alone. Without a $200 budget, it's certainly the one I'd be aiming for. But I fundamentally disagree with the sentiment that brands like Nacon just don't care about the gamepads they make because products like the Revolution 5 Unlimited and Revolution X Unlimited wouldn't be as good as they are without iteration, careful design, and years of expertise in their pedigree.

Coming from me, who struggles to justify any brand charging $200 for a controller, that should mean a lot. If you can afford this echelon of gamepad, there is no other controller I'd recommend more strongly. The longer I've spent with it through the RXU, and now its PlayStation sibling, the more I've come to appreciate what Nacon has made. With TMR improvements, the R5U has become the best controller on the shelves.

I've been using the Nacon Revolution X Unlimited for well over a year now, going back to it for comparisons to make in different bits of controller coverage, as well as for my own enjoyment of using it. I've got plenty of hands-on time and context with that gamepad, so I drew on that when it came time to test the R5U. I also compared it closely to the R5P, Nacon's previous PS5 controller. As you'll gather from the performance section of this review, I also used my hands-on time with lots of other gamepads to evaluate it.

All in all, I used the R5U in a slew of games and genres to try and see how versatile it is.

#3890. It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7

It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore.

US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7.

The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam.

With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week.

Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana. In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result.

The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass. Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers, though not always sales.

The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5, which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty, regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4.

Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been.

Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name.

"One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X. "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us."

Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

#3889. Goddess of Victory: Nikke's PC launcher suffers potential malware infection, with its publishers suggesting folks who've booted since late September do a security check

A cruel twist for the Shift Up-developed epic shooter RPG of cruel humanity destiny

Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a gacha shooter/RPG developed by Stellar Blade makers Shift Up, has suffered a "security incident" which has seen its PC launcher potentially be infected with third-party malware. Thankfully, it seems a patch to make the launcher safe again has been quickly dished out, but publishers Level Infinite are still advising players who've booted the game up since September 27th to do some security checks.

"We have identified that some files in the NIKKE Windows PC launcher were recently tampered with by a third party, potentially allowing malicious programs to run when the launcher was launched," the developers of the game with anime girls who - judging by the promo art - breast boobily announced yesterday. "As a result, your PCs and account information may have been exposed to security risks.

"We are continuing to investigate the extent of the potential damage and review appropriate response measures. We are also conducting a thorough review of our network security environment, including our CDN, to determine how the PC launcher files were compromised. We will take all necessary precautions to prevent further damage and ensure that this issue does not happen again. We deeply regret that this security incident has caused Commanders significant concern and distress, when our responsibility should have been to provide a safe gaming environment."

In order to try and help players "scan for and remove the malicious programs distributed in this incident", publishers Level Infinite have added a feature to Nikke's official PC client that does just that. They're advising that anyone who's booted up the game at least once after September 27th at 15:41 (UTC+9) use that or perform a manual security check.

Once that's done, affected players are advised to change the passwords for any accounts they've used on the PC they used to boot the launcher, as well as generate new API keys and access tokens. "We take very seriously the possibility that this incident may have affected not only your gaming experience but also your PC, accounts with external services, and personal assets," Level Infinite added. "If you believe you may have been affected by this issue or suffered from any loss, please contact our customer support team. We will review each inquiry carefully and respond as promptly as possible."

Going forwards, they plan to improve their monitoring "so that any unauthorized file modifications or security threats can be detected early and addressed promptly", as well as "establish an integrity verification system for external resources accessed by the PC launcher" and ensure the launcher only requires "the minimum permissions necessary".

Here's hoping the studio are able to keep things more secure in the future and that affected players are able to get rid of any malware with minimal suffering or inconvenience.

Ultima creator Richard Garriott was one of several developers on a recent panel hosted by the Georgia Game Developers Association, and Lord British was in fine form. Calling himself the "great-grandpa" of the group, he began by summarizing the current problems faced by the videogame industry.

"It's not just one thing," Garriott began. "I think if it was one thing it would be a lot easier to diagnose and come back from, but it's a lot of folks who don't understand videogames trying to make money off of videogames, it's a political climate, it's a billion things. All the threads have woven together into this horrible knot that we're seeing now."

He went on to describe a cycle he's seen play out multiple times over his years in the industry, where a technological advance comes along and everyone races to make a simple game that highlights that advance—whether it's the CD-ROM or a 3D-rendering pipeline or the internet—and only in the short gaps between these leaps forward is there much demand for something deeper.

"That cycle has been normal," Garriott said. "But we're at a new one, and this new one is machines are now fast enough to where the bells and whistles are no longer what's important." Without another advance having the same impact, he said, "we're at this kind of creative cliff where I think people don't know exactly what to do to prevent it and I think we've lost a lot of the original creators that were associated with those IPs and the bigger companies, and so I think we're floundering."

Garriott also had something to say about the way publishers have responded to the current state of the industry—by canceling games and laying off staff. Referring to his own publisher, Origin Systems, which he sold to EA in 1992, Garriott said, "Origin pre-EA, we never cancelled a project. Our theory was that if that team is capable of getting across the finish line, even if it doesn't sell well, they'll now know what it feels like to finish. And they will get feedback from the sales and the public as to what they did and didn't do right and so that team will be more strong, the individuals will be stronger, and we'll be able to circle back and do a more competent game next time.

"If you cancel a project, that means all those people on that team think you the publisher suck, because obviously their idea must've been brilliant, and so your willingness to cancel it was not their fault, but you the evil publisher. And half of them are probably going to leave or get fired, and maybe you'll scoop a few of them over into some other project that's now the priority project, but we thought that was a bad move on our own."

Things changed once EA snapped up Origin and took control, however. After that? "We canceled more projects than we completed by a long shot," Garriott said.

#3886. Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim

Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

Earlier this year, Electronic Arts was snapped up by a consortium including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and the investment firms Silver Lake and Affinity Partners in a deal worth $55 billion. According to Reuters, now the PIF and Silver Lake have their sights set on Unity Software, the company behind the multiplatform game engine of the same name.

Silver Lake is already one of Unity's bigger shareholders, owning roughly 8% of the company since investing around $400 million in it back in 2017. "Silver ​Lake’s Egon Durban also sits ⁠on Unity's board," as Reuters notes, "a dual role that would typically lead him to recuse himself from board deliberations on a sale."

The deliberations so far apparently include a valuation of about $25 billion, though since then Unity's most recent earnings report has come in, showing profits higher than estimated. Unity's come a long way since the Runtime Fee scandal, but it's not all about improvements to the engine like its ability to integrate with Unreal. As Reuters reports, "Strong ⁠growth in Unity's AI-powered Vector advertising platform helped it post its first quarterly profit on a GAAP basis since going public in September 2020."

The first thing that happened to EA after it was acquired was mass layoffs and being saddled with $18 billion of debt. I can't imagine anyone actually working at Unity has their fingers crossed for this deal to go through, but the videogame industry does seem determined to speedrun its way into a consolidation crisis where three consortiums own everything and almost everyone is unemployed.

#3884. Indie game website itch.io expands its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' continues to overwhelm Steam and other storefronts

Indie game storefront itch.io has expanded its AI disclosure filters, allowing its users to better separate games made with the controversial technology from those who don't.

This expansion, revealed on its official BlueSky account, includes Itchio's search page which now features a "No AI" box. By ticking this, users can hide any game on the website that features the generative AI disclosure. Games created using generative AI must have this disclosure to be present on the platform, similarly to Steam, although without an option to describe to what extent the tech was used.

This change comes shortly after itch.io also revealed the number of game pages being made on the website each day had doubled in the past two months. And, of course, the number of games downloaded and purchases have not doubled to match this new supply.

itch.io is also facing issues linked to the sheer file size. The storefront has a terms of service policy against AI spam, which it cited shortly after it publicly announced "a couple terabytes of AI slop" had been deleted.

This change comes as the industry as a whole has been clogged with an influx of AI games. Steam Next Fest had a record-breaking number of demo submissions last month. Developers pulled demos in fear of their game being copied, and with Steam saying it's the developer's responsibility to make their games less copyable.

It's an issue that isn't going away any time soon. Even as Claude creator Anthropic has introduced rules preventing unoriginal game clones, alternative AI tools can still be used to create them, and the process of creating games using AI tools will still allow for hastily made, low effort slop. Perhaps filters, like the one itch.io has expanded, is a workable solution to this on-going problem.

#3883. Apex Legends adds a grumpy, teamwiping Godzilla to its growing history of unappealing crossovers

No doubt eager as peas to help pay off EA's billions in debt, battle royale shooter Apex Legends is set to run another of its intellectual propertytastic crossover events. This one, starting on November 10th, stars Godzilla, of Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla vs. Kong, Godzilla (1954), Godzilla 2000: Millennium, Godzilla (1998), Son of Godzilla, and Godzilla (2014). I might be missing some.

Besides a profitable range of weapon and character skins, most of which appear to have hot glue gunned an 70-year film franchise's worth of dorsal fins all over themselves, the King of the Monsters himself will show up on the game's Storm Point map. He does at least have more than a background cameo: he'll occasionally blast an area with Legend-melting atomic breath, though brave souls who risk the danger zone can score a custom Devotion LMG with a unique heat ray attack of its own.

Worth noting also that the character skins are each based on a certain 'zilla movie, though as our freelance news writer and associate Large Lizard Cinema expert Ashley isn't working today, I'm not sure which of these are from hits and which are the duds. Walking wallhack motherfucker Bloodhound gets the newest fashion, their skin being inspired by Minus Zero, while my personal favourite Scottish scientist Horizon gets duds based on Big G in Godzilla vs. Destoroyah. Octane's skin is taken from... something called a Jet Jaguar? Google suggests this may in fact be elite Godzilla knowledge, something I clearly lack.

Regardless, and with the understanding that a lot of effort goes into these crossovers, I still kinda wish they didn't exist? Even putting aside basic game-playing problems with how, for example, wacky skins interfere with Legend silhouettes – you couldn't pay me to initiate a fight against a full team of near-identical Gundampeople - it's just icky to have an otherwise sharp, smart, at times fiercely competitive battle royale turned into an animated billboard for a few days.

Besides, Apex already has its own kaiju: the sleepy, pacifist Leviathans that innocently wandered into the King's Canyon map for a few of the earlier seasons. I consider these much better Friend Material than Godzilla, on the grounds that they'd only kill you by accident, and it was usually your own fault - by wandering under their briefly raised megahooves - anyway.
